DEAL TEAM REPORT — CHANGE OF CONTROL & ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS ANALYSIS
Target's Material Contracts — Acquisition Due Diligence
Corporate M&A | Matter File 8

PREPARED FOR: Deal Team / M&A Project Committee
PREPARED BY: Corporate M&A Practice
SUBJECT: Review of change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions across the Target's material contracts, including counterparty markup deviations flagged for analysis against firm precedent and market practice.

------------------------------------------------------------------
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------
We reviewed the acquisition data room contracts and the internal deal memo for change of control and assignment provisions across the Target's material contracts. The objective of this review is to identify (i) provisions that could trigger, restrict, or impede the proposed acquisition, (ii) consequences flowing from a change of control of the Target, (iii) transfer/assignment restrictions that could affect the assumption, novation, or assignment of contracts to or by the acquirer, and (iv) counterparty markup deviations that warrant negotiation in light of firm precedent and market practice.

Key findings:
• Multiple material contracts contain change of control provisions that could be triggered by the acquisition, including acceleration, termination, and consent requirements.
• Assignment provisions vary by contract type and counterparty; several contain "no assignment without consent" clauses that implicate post-closing internal restructuring and assumption mechanics.
• Counterparty's latest markup has introduced deviations from firm precedent and market practice in the definition of "change of control," the consent standard, and the scope of carve-outs; these require attention before signing.
• We flag the provisions requiring further analysis, negotiation priorities, and recommended positions.

------------------------------------------------------------------
II. SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY
------------------------------------------------------------------
Scope. This report covers the Target's material contracts in the acquisition data room, reviewed for change of control and assignment/transfer provisions. The review considered each contract's operative language, the internal memo, and the applicable regulatory and market framework.

Methodology. Each material contract was reviewed for:
• Definition of "change of control" (including control threshold, direct/indirect change, beneficial ownership, voting power, board composition);
• Change of control consequences (consent to be obtained, consent not to be unreasonably withheld, termination rights, acceleration/payment obligations, put/call rights, repurchase obligations);
• Assignment and transfer provisions (consent requirements, restrictions on assignment by operation of law, anti-assignment, novation requirements, permitted assignees/subsidiaries);
• Interaction between change of control and assignment clauses;
• Carve-outs (e.g., acquisition by a financial sponsor, merger of equals, internal restructuring, affiliate transfers).

------------------------------------------------------------------
III. KEY PROVISIONS IN THE OPERATIVE AGREEMENT
------------------------------------------------------------------
The operative agreement contains representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions negotiated between the parties. For change of control and assignment analysis, the following are the operative provisions of focus:

• Representations and Warranties: including no breach or violation of contracts upon a change of control, and accuracy of schedule listings of material contracts with CoC/assignment restrictions.
• Covenants: including run-of-business restrictions, restrictions on assignment of contracts prior to closing, and cooperation obligations to obtain third-party consents.
• Conditions to Closing: including receipt of required third-party consents to change of control/assignment as a condition precedent.
• Indemnification: allocation of risk for failure to obtain consents or for breach of CoC/assignment-related reps.
• Termination: rights of counterparties upon a change of control, and the "no-fault"/"with-cause" consent standards.

------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. FINDINGS — CHANGE OF CONTROL PROVISIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Definition of Change of Control
• Most contracts define a change of control by reference to (i) acquisition of more than 50% of voting power/equity, (ii) change in the majority of the board of directors, or (iii) sale of all or substantially all assets.
• A subset of contracts uses a lower threshold (e.g., 30% or "control" as defined) or a "beneficial ownership" trigger that could be implicated by the acquisition structure, including indirect ownership through the acquirer's holding structure.
• The counterparty's latest markup seeks to broaden the definition to capture indirect changes and to add a "material change in business" trigger, which departs from market practice and would widen the scope of contracts that could be deemed to have a change of control.

B. Change of Control Consequences
• Consent-based CoC clauses: counterparty consent required prior to a change of control. These create condition-precedent risk if consents are not obtained by closing.
• Termination-based CoC clauses: counterparty may terminate upon a change of control (with or without cause, with or without notice/cure). Termination could affect critical suppliers, customers, and IP licenses.
• Acceleration/payment-based CoC clauses: change of control triggers acceleration of payment obligations, prepayment, or repurchase, creating cash-flow and balance-sheet impact at closing.
• "Deemed assignment" provisions: a change of control may be deemed an assignment, bringing anti-assignment restrictions into operation.

C. Market Practice Observations
• Market-standard CoC consent provisions permit consent "not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed," and commonly include carve-outs for (i) acquisitions by a financial sponsor/PE fund and its affiliates, (ii) internal reorganizations, (iii) mergers resulting in continued existence of the Target, and (iv) public offerings.
• The counterparty markup removes or narrows these carve-outs and shifts the consent standard to "consent in counterparty's sole discretion," which is a material deviation requiring negotiation.

------------------------------------------------------------------
V. FINDINGS — ASSIGNMENT AND TRANSFER PROVISIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Consent to Assignment
• Several material contracts prohibit assignment, sale, or delegation of rights or obligations without the prior written consent of the counterparty.
• Certain contracts contain standalone "no assignment by operation of law" restrictions that would be triggered by a merger or consolidation.
• Assignability affects post-closing integration and the ability to transfer contracts into the acquirer's subsidiary structure without unnecessary administrative burden.

B. Permitted Assignees and Affiliate Transfers
• Some contracts permit assignment to wholly-owned subsidiaries or affiliates, provided the assignee assumes the obligations in writing. These reduce consent risk if the intended post-closing structure qualifies.
• The counterparty markup narrows permitted assignee language to require express consent even for affiliate transfers, increasing operational friction.

C. Novation Requirements
• For certain assignable contracts (e.g., key customer/supplier and IP license agreements), novation or a three-party consent may be required for assignment of the full benefit and burden.
• We recommend identifying contracts requiring novation and sequencing those consents before or at closing.

D. Interaction with Financing / Collateral Assignments
• Financing arrangements may permit security-interest assignments to lenders, but cross-default and acceleration provisions should be reconciled with CoC triggers.
• We flag any contract that restricts assignment to financing parties, as this can affect debt financing structures.

------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. OPEN ISSUES AND COUNTERPARTY MARKUP DEVIATIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
The following provisions have been flagged by counsel as requiring analysis against firm precedent and market practice, including deviations introduced by the counterparty's latest markup:

1. CoC Definition — the markup broadens the definition to include indirect changes and "material change in business," departing from firm precedent.
2. Consent Standard — the markup shifts from "consent not to be unreasonably withheld" to sole-discretion consent in key contracts.
3. Carve-Outs — the markup narrows or removes sponsor/affiliate/internal-reorganization carve-outs.
4. Termination Triggers — the markup adds termination rights upon any CoC with no cause or cure, which is aggressive relative to market.
5. Assignment to Affiliates — the markup requires express consent for affiliate transfers, creating integration friction.
6. Deemed Assignment — the markup treats certain restructurings as an assignment, expanding the scope of anti-assignment restrictions.

For each deviation, we recommend a negotiating position (accept / reject / counter) consistent with firm precedent and current market practice, as detailed below.

------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. RECOMMENDED POSITIONS AND NEGOTIATING PRIORITIES
------------------------------------------------------------------
Priority 1 — CoC Definition and Scope:
• Counter the broadened definition; propose a market-standard CoC definition tied to (i) >50% voting/equity, (ii) change of majority of the board, or (iii) sale of all or substantially all assets.
• Resist the "material change in business" trigger.

Priority 2 — Consent Standard:
• Reject sole-discretion consent; require consent "not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed."
• Establish a defined consent-request/response period to avoid closing delay.

Priority 3 — Carve-Outs:
• Preserve carve-outs for (i) acquisition by the buyer/financial sponsor and its affiliates, (ii) internal reorganizations, (iii) mergers where the Target survives, and (iv) public offerings.
• Ensure the acquisition structure qualifies for carve-outs to minimize required consents.

Priority 4 — Termination Triggers:
• Require that termination rights upon a change of control be limited to "material and adverse" breaches or include a cure period.
• Avoid unconditional, no-cause termination rights.

Priority 5 — Assignment/Affiliate Transfers:
• Maintain permitted-assignee language for wholly-owned subsidiaries/affiliates with written assumption of obligations.
• Reject express-consent requirements for qualifying affiliate transfers.

Priority 6 — Consents Condition Precedent:
• Negotiate that required third-party consents be a covenant (best-efforts/obligation to obtain) as well as a condition, with a clear remedy and potential for "sole risk" closing where available.

------------------------------------------------------------------
VIII. CONSENT TRACKING AND CONTRACT SCHEDULE
------------------------------------------------------------------
We recommend maintaining a consolidated consent/CoC matrix that lists, for each material contract:
• Contract name and counterparty
• CoC provision (present / absent), type, and threshold
• Consent requirement and standard (reasonable / sole discretion / none)
• Assignment restriction type
• Permitted assignees / carve-outs
• Termination/acceleration consequences
• Whether a consent/novation is required at closing, and status

This matrix should be kept current through closing and updated as consents are obtained or waivers secured.

------------------------------------------------------------------
IX. REGULATORY AND FRAMEWORK CONSIDERATIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
In analyzing CoC/assignment provisions, the deal team should consider the applicable regulatory framework, including:
• Duties and enforceability of consent-based CoC restrictions under governing law (including reasonableness requirements for restrictions that are not freely assignable).
• Anti-assignment clauses and their enforceability, including the "silence" rule and the effect of operation-of-law assignments.
• Interaction with stock purchase vs. asset purchase structure (asset deals may require separate consents for each assigned contract).
• Compliance with any filings or regulatory approvals (e.g., HSR/competition, sectoral approvals) that may be conditions to the change of control.

------------------------------------------------------------------
X. CONCLUSION
------------------------------------------------------------------
The Target's material contracts collectively present moderate-to-high change of control and assignment risk that must be managed. The most significant exposures arise from (i) broadened CoC definitions and sole-discretion consent standards in the counterparty's latest markup, (ii) termination/acceleration rights that could be triggered at closing, and (iii) assignment restrictions that affect post-closing integration. We recommend (a) negotiating the flagged deviations back toward firm precedent and market practice, (b) building a prioritized consent/novation matrix with a closing condition plan, and (c) preserving reasonable consent and carve-out protections. With disciplined negotiation and consent tracking, the deal can proceed with manageable and allocable risk.

Prepared by the Corporate M&A team for the deal committee. This report is privileged and confidential, prepared in connection with the proposed acquisition and in anticipation of litigation.
